The mechanism of the synergistic effect of microstructural evolution on fracture toughness in low-density
δ-ferrite steel under varying rolling temperatures was systematically investigated in this study. The findings
indicated that a lamellar microstructure can be formed through high-temperature rolling (850–950 <sup>◦</sup>C), con
sisting of δ-ferrite, honeycomb martensite lamellae, and equiaxed ferrite grains which are formed by DIFT
(deformation-induced ferrite phase transformation) within the honeycomb structure. Together with the con:
centration of interfacial stress, the equiaxed DIF (deformation induced ferrite) grains served as pre-existing
defects, resulting in an impact energy of less than 7 J at room temperature (elongation less than 9 %). Mean

ferrite was formed by low-temperature rolling (650–750 <sup>◦</sup>C). Under the influence of the Orowan mechanism,

deflect horizontally and extended the propagation path. At the same time, the presence of these carbides

carbides also promoted horizontal crack propagation along lamellar boundaries. These multiple mechanisms
collectively enhanced material toughness, resulting in an impact absorption energy of up to 207.5 J (elongation
19.8 %). These results suggested a new pathway for the strength-toughness regulation of lightweight steel.

the stable presence of coarse δ-ferrite (grain size >50 μm) at room

cubic) phase, has a limited number of slip systems and lacks phase
transformation refinement mechanisms, making grain refinement and
microstructure optimization difficult by traditional heat treatment
[8–10]. Studies have shown that when the volume fraction of δ-ferrite
exceeds 20 vol%, the impact toughness decreases by more than 60 %,
which becomes a bottleneck restricting the engineering application of
low-density steel [11,12].
To overcome the limitation of low toughness in low-density δ-ferrite
steel, thermomechanical processing (e.g., rolling) is adopted in δ-ferrite
grain refinement and microstructure configuration design. Through hot
rolling, DRX (dynamic recrystallization) occurs to refine grains, with
simultaneous phase interface regulation enabling the construction of a
lamellar microstructure to balance strength, plasticity, and toughness. In
recent years, lamellar structures have shown exceptional performance.
Three typical microstructures are categorized to illustrate this design
concept. The first category refers to the ferrite/martensite dual-phase
lamellar structure. Zhang et al. [13] achieved an interphase constraint
effect to inhibit localized deformation via hot rolling, obtaining excel
lent mechanical properties with a yield strength (YS) of 700 MPa and a
TE (total elongation) of 25 %. Similarly, Cao et al. [14] prepared a
ferrite/martensite dual-phase lamellar structure via hot rolling, and the
structure has an impact absorption energy of 300–450 J. The second
category is characterized by multi-phase lamellar structure (e.g.,
martensite matrix + ultra-fine retained austenite + oriented δ-ferrite
lamellae), Hu et al. [15] realized the synergistic improvement of me
chanical properties, with an UTS (ultimate tensile strength) of 2112 MPa
and TE of 16 %, via hot rolling and tempering. Thirdly, the introduction
of second-phase particles is widely applied to enhance the mechanical
properties of materials, Prasad et al. [16] introduced ultra-fine spherical
cementite into the material through multi-pass warm rolling and
annealing, achieving a UTS ≥825 MPa and TE of 30 %.

Based on the aforementioned studies, as a core process parameter,
rolling temperature directly dominates phase composition, interface
characteristics, and defect distribution. Furthermore, existing research
has a gap, which concerns the micro-mechanism of spherical carbides in
lamellar structures interacting with crack paths to influence toughness.
To address this gap, this study aims to investigate the effect of spherical
carbides on mechanical properties and impact fracture behavior in
lamellar microstructures. Focusing on low-density δ-ferrite steel, this
work systematically establishes the relationship among rolling temper
ature, carbide evolution, and crack propagation behavior through multi-
scale microstructure characterization and mechanical property testing.
Recently, we have developed DRX kinetics studies through thermo
mechanical deformation experiment [17], where different rolling tem
peratures were selected to cover the temperature ranges of carbide
precipitation/dissolution, DRX, and DIFT. Previous efforts to improve
the mechanical properties of δ-ferrite lightweight steel have typically
focused on grain refinement of δ-ferrite via DRX. While
high-temperature rolling can induce DRX for grain refinement, it also
triggers phenomena such as DIFT, exerting unpredictable impacts on
material properties. Thus, compared with martensite/δ-ferrite lamellar
steel formed by high-temperature rolling, a rolling process that mini
mally induces DRX and DIFT is urgently required.
The innovation of this study lies in recognizing the phenomenon that
second-phase particles dispersedly distributed in the microstructure can
enhance the strain hardening capacity of steel, and combining spherical
carbide strengthening with lamellar structure strengthening [18], and
this novel lamellar structure also meets the requirement for formation at
lower rolling temperatures. Furthermore, this integration establishes the
correlation between work hardening behavior and microstructure,
which links precipitate characteristics to fracture behavior via theoret
ical models (e.g., Orowan model). The synergistic mechanism of dislo
cation storage and second-phase strengthening is deduced in reverse by
analyzing the features of θ-curves (work hardening rate vs. true strain).
The multi-stage toughening mechanism of carbides in the
low-temperature rolling zone is revealed through microstructure anal
ysis as follows: ultra-fine spherical carbides induce crack tip blunting,
crack deflection, and microvoid nucleation to trigger horizontal crack
propagation. These effects dissipate energy and enable the impact en
ergy to exceed 200 J. Meanwhile, the causes of brittle fracture in sam
ples from the high-temperature rolling zone were analyzed. It was
found, by combining EBSD (electron backscatter diffraction) analysis
with nanoindentation tests, that equiaxed grains of DIF within
honeycomb-like martensite lamellae act as “prefabricated crack paths”.
Stress concentration also exists at the phase interface, and the two
jointly induce brittle fracture.

2.2. Mechanical tests and microstructure study
Mechanical property tests included tensile tests and Charpy impact
tests. Tensile tests were performed using rod-shaped specimens with a
gauge length of 25 mm and a diameter of 5 mm, which were sampled
along the rolling direction (RD) of the plate. The tensile test was con-
ducted at a crosshead speed of 1.5 mm/min. The specimens used for the
Charpy impact test were Charpy V-notch samples with dimensions of 10
mm × 10 mm × 55 mm. The notch was machined on the rolled surface,
and the impact direction was perpendicular to the RD. The geometry of
the Charpy impact specimens and tensile specimens are illustrated in
Fig. 1b and c. Multi-scale microstructure characterization was per-
formed using the following techniques. Firstly, for SEM (scanning
electron microscopy) and EBSD analyses, the model of the experimental
equipment and the sample preparation method were as follows: An
Apreo S HiVac SEM equipped with an Oxford Aztec EBSD detector was
used, and all observations were conducted on the RD-ND (Normal Di
rection) plane. After grinding and polishing, SEM samples were etched
with a 5 vol % HNO₃-ethanol solution to reveal their microstructural
features; EBSD samples were electro-polished using a 5 vol%

the ferrite lamellae, forming a microstructure with alternating
arrangement with δ-ferrite lamellae; a small amount existed as short
rod-like cementite at the ferrite grain boundaries. In the impact test,
cracks initiated and propagated from the V-notch. They exhibited a
plane strain state in the δ-ferrite lamellae, as the δ-ferrite grains were
coarse and had low hardness—this caused stress concentration at the
crack tip and enabled the crack to quickly penetrate this region. When
the crack propagated to the carbide/ferrite lamellae, it showed a plane
stress state. Interface separation occurred during crack propagation,
which dispersed the stress at the crack tip on the interface separation
surface, reducing stress concentration and making it difficult for the
crack to further propagate vertically through the lamellae. Meanwhile,
due to high-deformation rolling, the crack needed to pass through
numerous lamellae to propagate along the ND, resulting in a significant
increase in energy dissipation.

As shown in Fig. 8d, the crack tip became significantly blunted and
stopped propagating while penetrating the carbide/ferrite lamellae.
This is due to carbides in the lamellae release local stress in the ferrite
grains while maintaining good interfacial incompatibility, making it
difficult for stress to concentrate in the early stage and for cracks to
propagate. According to Griffith's microcrack theory [31] and EET
theory [32], the bonding force at the carbide/ferrite interface in the
carbide/ferrite lamellae is greater than that at the ferrite/ferrite inter
face, and the presence of numerous nanoscale spherical carbides can
effectively prevent cracks from passing through the carbide/ferrite
lamellae. Meanwhile, Du et al. [33] found that precipitated nanoscale
spherical carbidess (hard phases) can blunt the crack tip and exhibit
excellent crack propagation resistance. Additionally, this phenomenon
also originates from the dispersion of stress concentration at the crack
tip by spherical carbide particles. When the crack propagates near the
spherical particles, the smooth surface of the particles interacts with the
crack, increasing the effective curvature radius of the crack tip and thus
preventing stress concentration.
According to the theory of elasticity, the stress concentration factor is
inversely proportional to the curvature radius—an increase in radius
directly reduces the local stress peak at the crack tip, and the synergistic
effect of numerous particles enhances the blunting effect [34]. In addi
tion, during the impact process, spherical carbides act as nucleation sites
for microvoids (Fig. 8f), inducing the formation of microvoids and
microcracks at the carbide/ferrite interfaces. These secondary defects
mainly propagate along the horizontal direction of the lamellae
(Fig. 8g), releasing the concentrated high stress and thus improving the
plasticity and toughness. Compared with the research by Zhang et al.
[35], dispersedly distributed spherical carbides can both improve the
mechanical properties of materials via the Orowan mechanism. How
ever, unlike the spherical carbides formed by the spheroidization of
lamellar cementite in Zhang's study, the nanoscale spherical carbides in
this work are derived from martensite decomposition, featuring smaller
size, more complete sphericity, and more uniform distribution. Conse
quently, they better demonstrate the Orowan mechanism.
Microstructural analysis of the tensile deformation zone of low:
temperature rolling zone specimens revealed that carbide/ferrite
lamellae exerted a significant positive regulatory effect on the material's
UTS, TE and SPP. Firstly, the dispersed distribution of ultrafine spherical
carbides induced a dispersion strengthening effect, effectively
enhancing material strength. Further observation indicated that crack
propagation was confined within δ-ferrite lamellae and ran parallel to
the lamellar orientation (Fig. 8h-i). The presence of nanoscale carbide
enabled carbide/ferrite lamellae to form a barrier-like obstruction [33,
34], greatly improving crack penetration resistance and forcing crack
to propagate along longer paths within δ-ferrite lamellae. On this basis,
the ultrafine spherical carbides in the R650 specimen, with smaller size
and higher distribution density, exhibited more pronounced dispersion
strengthening and crack inhibition effects, making the UTS, TE and SPP
of R650 superior to those of R750. Meanwhile, this lamellar structure
consisting of hard phases (carbide/ferrite) and soft phases (δ-ferrite)
possessed excellent deformation coordination capability [9],namely
that the soft δ-ferrite lamellae provided sufficient space for plastic
deformation, effectively coordinating the deformation constraints of
hard phase lamellae and avoiding local stress concentration. Under the
combined action of these mechanisms, cracks extended to varying de
grees along δ-ferrite lamellae, substantially increasing energy con
sumption during crack propagation and thus delaying the fracture
process. Eventually, the tensile fractures of the specimens displayed a
typical serrated morphology with delamination characteristics (Fig. 8c),
which accounted for the excellent comprehensive TE and SPP properties
of specimens from the low-temperature rolling zone.
Fig. 9a-d shows the TEM images of the impact-fractured deformation
zone of R650, along with the HRTEM (high-resolution transmission
electron microscopy) and IFFT (inverse fast fourier transform) images of
selected carbide regions. As observed in Fig. 9a and c, after impact
deformation, numerous dislocations were blocked by carbides and piled
up in the regions adjacent to carbides. Fig. 9b and d are HRTEM images
of the carbide regions, where dark areas represent carbides and light
areas correspond to the ferrite matrix. Inverse Fourier transform was
performed on the ferrite/carbide boundaries to obtain IFFT filtered
images. Analysis of the dislocation characteristics reveals that when
carbide diameter exceeds 10 nm, numerous dislocations and atomic
shearing are observed at the ferrite/carbide boundaries. This is because
the Orowan mechanism [36,37] hinders dislocation movement, thereby
strengthening the lamellae. Meanwhile, part of the interfacial stress
between the ferrite matrix and carbides is transferred to the carbides,
alleviating interfacial stress concentration and making it difficult for
cracks to propagate through the lamellae containing carbides—this
improves the fracture toughness of the material. Based on the above
mechanisms, the fracture mode exhibits a mixed pattern (Fig. 9e and h):
on one hand, crack blunting makes it difficult for cracks to propagate
perpendicular to the lamellae; on the other hand, lamellar separation
and secondary defects induce cracks to propagate along the direction of
lamellar separation.
In the R750 specimen, the carbide content decreases significantly
and the particle size coarsens, as shown in Fig. 3e-f. Although the R750
and R650 specimens have similar microstructural morphologies and
comparable hardness of each phase, there is still a significant difference
in their impact absorption energy. It can be inferred that the difference
in carbides plays a crucial role in the material's fracture behavior at thi
point. The decrease in carbide proportion and particle coarsening are
likely key reasons for the significant weakening of the toughening effect.
This change in carbides leads to a reduction in crack deflection resis
tance, making it easier for cracks to propagate in a straight line and thus
lowering energy absorption. It also affects the blunting effect: coarse
particles have a weakened ability to disperse stress at the crack tip, and
the reduced tip curvature radius causes an increase in the stress intensity
factor. Meanwhile, the decrease in carbide quantity results in lower
carbide density and larger spacing, reducing the number of sites that
hinder dislocation movement and overall weakening the Orowan
mechanism. Finally, the number of microvoid nucleation sites in the
horizontal direction decreases; fewer ultra-fine carbides lead to less
microcrack initiation, weakening the energy dissipation mechanism of
secondary cracks. Therefore, the impact absorption energy of R750
decreased by approximately 60 % compared with R650, and its fracture
mode is shown in Fig. 9f and i.
The microstructures of R850 and R950 undergo a fundamental
transformation, in which carbides are completely dissolved, forming a
dual-phase structure consisting of δ-ferrite lamellae and honeycomb
martensite lamellae. Moreover, equiaxed grains obtained via DIFT are
embedded within the honeycomb martensite lamellae, creating a hon
eycomb structure (Fig. 9g). At this point, the impact absorption energy
of the test steel decreases significantly (<10 J), which is caused by the
following aspects. First is interfacial stress concentration. There are
significant hardness differences between the martensite phase, δ-ferrite,
and DIF, which weakens the bonding at phase interfaces and leads to
more concentrated stress at the crack tip. Second is the “crack propa
gation shortcut” effect of DIF. The equiaxed ferrite grains act as pre-
existing defects, guiding cracks to propagate rapidly in a cleavage
mode, which significantly reduces energy consumption. Third is the
high brittleness of honeycomb martensite lamellae, which inhibits
plastic deformation and causes a sharp decrease in fracture toughness.
Its fracture schematic is shown in Fig. 9j, which conforms to the char
acteristics of typical brittle fracture. This confirms that high-
temperature rolling significantly degrades material toughness through
microstructure coarsening and the formation of brittle phases.
